flashcards.front: Why must all input be treated as untrusted?
flashcards.back_definition: Anything a user, client or other system sends can be crafted by an attacker: form fields, URLs, headers, cookies, JSON and uploaded files.
flashcards.back_example: An attacker changes a hidden price field from 499 to 1 before submitting.
flashcards.back_confusion: Validation in the browser improves usability but gives no security; check again on the server.

flashcards.back_definition: An allowlist accepts only input matching a known-good pattern. A denylist rejects known-bad patterns and must anticipate every variant, so it is weaker.
flashcards.back_example: Allowlist: a UK postcode must match the postcode format and nothing else.
flashcards.back_confusion: Attackers bypass denylists with case changes, encoding and alternate syntax.
flashcards.back_hook: Name the good, not every bad.

flashcards.back_definition: Converting input to one standard form before validating it, so encoded or disguised variants can't slip past.
flashcards.back_example: %2e%2e%2f decodes to ../; decode first, then check for path traversal.
flashcards.back_confusion: Validating the raw string before decoding lets double-encoded attacks through.

flashcards.back_definition: Sanitisation strips or rewrites dangerous content when input arrives. Output encoding transforms data for the specific place it is used (HTML, SQL, shell, JSON).
flashcards.back_example: The same name is HTML-encoded on a web page and passed as a parameter to SQL.
flashcards.back_confusion: One clean-up on arrival can't fit every later context; encode at each use.
flashcards.back_hook: Clean on entry, encode on exit.

flashcards.back_definition: Parameterised queries, output encoding, secrets kept out of code, least privilege for the app and its database account, and managing and patching dependencies.
flashcards.back_example: The app connects as a database user that can't drop tables, with its password in a secrets manager.
flashcards.back_confusion: Code that passes every functional test can still be insecure.
flashcards.back_hook: Parameterise, encode, hide secrets, limit rights, patch libraries.

flashcards.back_definition: When something goes wrong, the code denies access by default and reveals as little as possible.
flashcards.back_example: If the permission check throws an error, the request is refused, not allowed.
flashcards.back_confusion: Detailed stack traces shown to users hand attackers reconnaissance.

flashcards.back_definition: A vulnerable third-party library makes your application vulnerable, so you need to track versions and patch them.
flashcards.back_example: Log4Shell (CVE-2021-44228) in the Log4j logging library affected huge numbers of Java applications in December 2021.
flashcards.back_confusion: You inherit the bugs of every library you ship.
flashcards.back_hook: Your code is only as safe as its dependencies.

flashcards.back_definition: SAST analyses source code without running it, early in the pipeline. DAST attacks the running application from outside, so it needs a deployed instance.
flashcards.back_example: SAST flags string-built SQL; DAST finds a reflected XSS on the live search page.
flashcards.back_confusion: They find different problems; mature pipelines use both.
flashcards.back_hook: SAST reads the recipe; DAST tastes the dish.

flashcards.front: What can't SAST or DAST find?
flashcards.back_definition: Business-logic flaws and chains of small issues, which need human penetration testers who understand what the app is meant to do.
flashcards.back_example: Applying the same discount coupon twice to get a negative total.
flashcards.back_confusion: A clean scan means no known patterns were found, not that the app is secure.
flashcards.back_hook: Tools find patterns; people find plots.

flashcards.front: Why run security tests in the CI/CD pipeline?
flashcards.back_definition: Every change is checked automatically, so problems are caught early when they are cheapest to fix.
flashcards.back_example: A merge request is blocked because SAST finds a hardcoded API key.
flashcards.back_confusion: Automation adds checks; it does not replace review and testing by people.
flashcards.back_hook: Test every change, not every year.

flashcards.front: Secure by design vs secure by default?
flashcards.back_definition: Secure by design builds security into the architecture from the start. Secure by default ships with the safest settings already on, so users don't have to harden it themselves.
flashcards.back_example: A product that forces a new admin password at first login and has MFA turned on.
flashcards.back_confusion: Bolting security on after release costs more and misses design flaws.

flashcards.front: How did the 2018 British Airways attack work?
flashcards.back_definition: Attackers modified a JavaScript file on BA's payment page (a Magecart attack) to copy card details to their own server. The UK ICO fined BA £20 million.
flashcards.back_example: About 22 lines of added script skimmed card details for roughly two weeks in August and September 2018.
flashcards.back_confusion: A Content Security Policy and Subresource Integrity could have blocked or detected the changed script.
flashcards.back_hook: A skimmer, but made of JavaScript.

flashcards.front: What do a Content Security Policy and Subresource Integrity do?
flashcards.back_definition: CSP tells the browser which sources may load scripts and other content. SRI adds a hash to a script tag so the browser refuses a modified file.
flashcards.back_example: <script src="lib.js" integrity="sha384-..."> fails to load if lib.js is changed.
flashcards.back_confusion: These are defence in depth; they do not replace fixing XSS in the code.
flashcards.back_hook: Only approved scripts, only unchanged scripts.
